chapter: Big bands, small groups and studio work
title: Big band versus small group drumming

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: One thing I wanted to ask you. You had a chance to do both a good deal of both small group and big band work, you know, and I guess you always have. What do you see as the difference between those two idioms? How do you approach each one?
The big band and the what you mean the ad lib groups or the small groups or....
Or, I guess the ad lib groups, when you're saying the big band, well--
Big band as opposed to a small group.

Well a big band is mostly if you have charts to play, you've got to stick to the chart as close as you can. Of course, little things, I mean you've got to ad lib on you know, you just can't play a chart exactly as it's written. It's just like Duke said, after an arrangement is a thing there that is, notes that will guide everybody in the right direction. Now after you learn, or after you play the notes, everybody gets acquainted with the notes, your da! segno signs, the structure, the whole arrangement, now after everybody plays their arrangement down, now the thing to do is let's put some character to that arrangement, bend
the note here, bend the note there. See...
The ironic thing with Duke is that he didn't write any drum parts.

No, that's right, and well so Sonny knew backwards and Louie Bellson too, you know, and then the charts. Now, see, music is music, a whole note's a whole note wherever it is, I have no dotted quarter, dotted sixteenth, whatever you want to do, call it. A note's a note. Now you've got to adapt yourself to, first you should know what a big band should sound like, a drummer when he sits in with a big band, first thing he's got to figure is what can he do to enhance that arrangement that this big band is doing. Now he can stick to his charts, he can have his drum chart written out there, but a lot of little things he can do, little kick beats that he can do that will enhance the whole band, and anybody see, any well schooled musician can sit down and play note after note, but it'll sound very stiff if that's all you're doing is just playing what's written on that paper, note after note, sometimes it'll sound good, if it's a saxophone chorus and the saxophones are all breathing together and you take the breath at the same time or brass or whatever. And that will sound good, but everybody just to sit up there and just play those notes as they're written. Say like if you have four quarter notes .... all right now maybe in that arrangement you can bend those notes a little bit ... and sort of bend them a little, put little slurs over them.

That's the thing that I'm talking about, you've got to add character to them. Now, with a small group, the way I do, you sit down and you start playing with a small group and then you listen. You've got to have those ears going all the time, you listen. You'll take a solo. If you take one solo, I get an idea of how you play. If you take two, I get a better idea of how you're playing, and so you go on from there, and whereas you're liable to say (HUMMING), well see with me drumming, I'm liable to say (HUMMING), to enhance what you are doing, but stay out of your way, I don't want to take the solo away from you, I'm not going to play solo drums behind your solo, but I'm going to feed you a certain foundation that will make you feel good while you're playing, and I've heard so many drummers, especially drummers play and somebody is up there taking a solo. Well they're playing so loud that you can't hear the solo, or maybe they're up there trying to play a drum solo along with the soloist, and that's no good, I don't think.
If I had a dollar for every time I've had gigs messed up by bad drummers or insensitive drummers or both ....
